Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) is a pay-as-you-go service based on the volume of emails sent and received. There are no contract negotiations and no upfront commitments.

Amazon will really quickly suspend your SES account if your bounce rate is too high. They also don't keep hugely detailed logs, so restoring service generally relies on you keeping good logs from your app/MTA.
I moved to AWS SES for inbound emails. I wrote a small Lambda function which dissects the email and forwards it to my HTTP endpoint. With usage growing, SES was getting expensive as well.
SES only has 1 feature in common with Mailchimp and that is the sending of an email. Mailchimp's primary function is managing distribution lists, email templates and receiver activity analytics.
We switched from MailChimp to SES+Email Octopus. EO gives us the layout+list management stuff we needed, and SES gave us a huge drop in mail sending cost.

Having used both I love SES. It's great... One big gripe I have with SES is that it tends to have more servers on spam blacklists than Mailchimp. You also need to code a lot of the stuff Mailchimp has out of the box (like templates and delivery reports) yourself... Another great thing SES has is the ability to receive emails not just send.
I've just started using SES and did notice everything going to spam. Looking for a solution.
Mailchimp === great UI for ad hoc newsletters. SES === great for transactional emails if you handle the templating yourself.

Aaaaaand that's why I no longer use Amazon SES for transactional mail... It is frequently used by mass-marketers, which means my transactional email was frequently being dropped by some email providers because of SES's poor deliverability.

Years ago we started with AWS SES. The pricing was amazing but there was no useful customer service outlet. If you were sending via a blacklisted IP it could be weeks before you were seeing inbox reliability again... we devote 20+ man hours per week dealing with email issues while using AWS.

In my experience Amazon SES is great if you only used it for transactional emails. If you start sending marketing emails you will soon find yourself being blocked by ISPs... Some service providers will even block the domain name.

Anyone who uses Amazon SES knows deliverability isn't that great. When you use mailchimp you're practically paying for a higher chance for any of your emails not ending up in the spambox (even if they're transactional).

Lot of the IPs used by SES are already blocked because somebody used it for spamming... The most annoying part is it's not deterministic, sometimes it works sometimes gmail blocks it or puts into spam.

I made the same move last year for my mailing list... using Amazon SES as the e-mail sending service. It ended up saving me $600/year back then and would - at this point - be saving me roughly $2,000/year.

SES is more like outsourcing sendmail on your own server so you don't carry the burden of maintaining/securing it, except that you don't have control over it when something goes wrong... If you value your messages getting to the inbox, it's the least desirable option.
The only bummer with SES for serious newsletter folks is that you can't get a dedicated IP address.
Amazon SES will place your account under review if your bounce rate is 5% or greater.

Most of the Amazon SES IP blacklisted by SpamCannibal... The SES team knows about the spam cannibal listings and is in contact with them, they say it's unlikely your open rate drop from 25% to 0.15% is caused by the SC listing.
I had had the same issue with amazon SES. Due to the default configuration error, all the emails we send out ended up in spam. Finally, the issue got fixed by configuring reverse PTR.
Holy shit. There goes any reluctance I had to building on top of SES. Your move, Sendgrid.

We had already decided to go with MailChimp for our bulk email needs and have been on the fence about Amazon SES vs SendGrid. But with us already leaning toward Amazon SES, this pretty much just seals the deal.
